case.title: Downstream Fuels Replenishment: Turn a Vague Sponsor Request into Traceable Requirements, a Backlog, and a System Gap Analysis
case.brief: You are the Business Analyst newly assigned to the Downstream Supply & Distribution unit of an integrated oil & gas company. The Supply Chain Planning Lead has raised a request to 'fix' how the team replenishes regional fuel terminals (MOGAS, diesel, jet) from refineries and import jetties: planners run weekly schedules in spreadsheets, terminals occasionally stock out, and the logistics team is absorbing avoidable demurrage on vessels and standing time on road tankers. The sponsor has asked the delivery team for 'an automated replenishment dashboard.' Your job over the next ~1.5 hours is to do real BA work on this request — not to build software, and not to accept the request at face value. You have a small set of intake and discovery materials in repoSeed; they are a constructed-but-realistic scenario standing in for the kind of artifacts you'd inherit on day one (no real client documents were available, so treat these as your only ground truth). Work as you would inside an Agile/Scrum delivery team using MS Azure DevOps. Deliverables are short and written — clarity and judgment matter far more than length. Where the materials are silent, contradictory, or surprising, that is the work: make a defensible call, write it down, and note what you'd confirm with the team. Output a single Markdown document (sections per task) plus the requested CSV-style backlog rows; you do not need running code or diagrams beyond simple text/notation (swimlane-in-text is fine).
case.repoSeed:
A discovery pack handed over from the sponsor and the prior planning team:

- intake/replenishment-planning-request.md — a one-page intake note from the Supply Chain Planning Lead. States the ask as 'an automated replenishment dashboard so planners stop running out of stock,' sets headline targets ('cut stockouts by 30% and demurrage by 20% this year'), and quotes two stakeholders whose priorities differ: Planning wants better demand-forecast accuracy; Logistics/Scheduling wants fewer demurrage events. The note conflates the symptom (stockouts/demurrage) with a specific solution (a dashboard), and the two demurrage figures it cites (one in the body, one in a footnote table) don't match.

- current-state/replenishment-process-narrative.md — a 1.5-page narrative of how weekly replenishment planning works today: demand pulled from history into Excel, manual safety-stock rules, schedules emailed to the scheduling desk, re-work when vessels slip. One paragraph mentions, almost in passing, that a demand-planning module ('DP Optimizer') was purchased and configured ~18 months ago for exactly this forecasting need but was 'switched off after the rollout didn't land' (cited reasons: poor master-data quality and low planner adoption).

- systems/capability-inventory.csv — a system × capability matrix for the enterprise landscape: SAP S/4HANA (ERP/inventory/orders), Oracle Transportation Management (TMS — scheduling, demurrage tracking), DP Optimizer (statistical demand planning add-on, marked 'Inactive'), Power BI (reporting), and 'Excel/manual' rows. Columns flag whether each system Supports / Partially supports / Doesn't support capabilities like demand forecasting, safety-stock policy, vessel/truck scheduling, demurrage capture, and days-of-cover reporting. The DP Optimizer row shows it already supports the forecasting capability the sponsor is asking to acquire.

- data/terminal-inventory-demand-2024W08-W11.csv — a four-week extract for ~6 terminals: columns terminal_id, product, opening_inventory_m3, receipts_MT, lifted_MT, demand_forecast_MT. Inventory is recorded in cubic metres (m³) while receipts, liftings and demand are in metric tonnes (MT); there is no conversion column and product densities differ (MOGAS ≈ 0.74 t/m³, diesel ≈ 0.84 t/m³, jet ≈ 0.80 t/m³). A naive 'days of cover = inventory / demand' computed straight off these columns looks reasonable but is unit-inconsistent and product-dependent.

- backlog/azure-devops-export.csv — a small export of existing Azure DevOps work items, including an open epic 'EPIC-142 Replenishment Optimisation' owned by Solution Architecture that partially overlaps this new request, plus a few stale/mislabelled stories beneath it.
tasks: 1) Frame the problem (≈15–20 min). Using intake/replenishment-planning-request.md and the current-state narrative, separate the underlying business problem from the proposed solution. State the problem in one or two sentences, list your top 4–6 assumptions, and write the 5–8 highest-value clarifying questions you would take to the sponsor and the two named stakeholders before committing scope — ordered by how much each would change the solution. Call out explicitly any place where Planning's and Logistics' stated priorities pull in different directions.

2) Requirements & backlog (≈25–30 min). Produce a prioritised set of business requirements (MoSCoW or equivalent) traceable to the problem above, then express the Must/Should items as 4–6 Azure DevOps user stories with acceptance criteria, sized for a sprint backlog. Each story must trace back to a stated business requirement (give the trace). Keep acceptance criteria testable and free of solution lock-in where the solution is still open.

3) Gap analysis & options (≈20–25 min). Map your requirements against systems/capability-inventory.csv to show fit, partial fit and genuine gaps. Then recommend at least two solution options with explicit trade-offs (e.g. reuse/rehabilitate an existing capability, configure/extend, build new, or change the process) and a recommendation with rationale. Be specific about what the existing landscape can already do versus what is truly missing.

4) Process, data validation & DECISIONS log (≈20–25 min). Sketch a current-state vs target-state replenishment process (text swimlane or simple notation is fine) showing where the solution intervenes. Then validate data/terminal-inventory-demand-2024W08-W11.csv well enough to trust a 'days of cover' metric: state whether the extract can be used as-is, and if not, what must change and how that affects your requirements. Throughout all four tasks, keep a short DECISIONS log — a normal part of how we work — with one row per open call you made: what you chose, the alternative you rejected, and the question you'd put to the team to confirm it.

coverProbes.where: intake/replenishment-planning-request.md — the ask is 'an automated replenishment dashboard,' with Planning and Logistics stating different priorities
coverProbes.reveals: A good candidate reframes a stated solution ('a dashboard') back to the business problem (stockouts + demurrage + their root causes), surfaces the Planning-vs-Logistics tension as a real scope decision, and refuses to spec a UI before the objective is agreed. A naive candidate writes a dashboard specification and inherits the sponsor's framing wholesale, optimising for the wrong outcome.
decisionSpace: Scope to the requested dashboard and deliver fast — satisfies the sponsor's literal ask and shows momentum, but risks polishing a symptom and not moving stockouts/demurrage.
Reframe to the underlying stockout/demurrage problem and propose measuring root cause before committing to any UI — higher long-term value, but slower and may read as not delivering what was asked.
Split the work: a thin reporting quick-win now plus a parallel root-cause/forecast workstream — manages both stakeholders, but costs coordination and can dilute focus.

coverProbes.where: current-state/replenishment-process-narrative.md (the 'switched off after rollout' aside) cross-referenced with the 'Inactive' DP Optimizer row in systems/capability-inventory.csv
coverProbes.reveals: A good candidate reads the materials before generating, notices the forecasting capability the sponsor wants to 'acquire' already exists but was abandoned, and reframes the problem as adoption + master-data quality rather than a missing tool. A naive candidate, generating from the headline ask, proposes buying or building new forecasting and silently re-creates the conditions of the prior failure.
decisionSpace: Recommend rehabilitating DP Optimizer — lowest cost and reuses a paid asset, but inherits the data-quality and adoption problems that killed it unless those are tackled first.
Recommend a fresh build/buy — clean slate and full control, but ignores the sunk asset and the unaddressed root causes that would sink a new tool too.
Recommend a short, time-boxed diagnostic on why DP Optimizer failed before choosing — de-risks the decision, but adds a step before any visible delivery and needs sponsor patience.

coverProbes.where: data/terminal-inventory-demand-2024W08-W11.csv — inventory in m³, flows/demand in MT, no conversion, product-dependent density; plus the mismatched demurrage figures in the intake note
coverProbes.reveals: A good candidate verifies the data before building metrics on it: spots that 'days of cover = inventory / demand' mixes m³ and MT, that the conversion depends on per-product density, flags the inconsistent demurrage baseline, and adds a data-quality requirement. A naive one-shot answer computes a plausible-looking days-of-cover that passes a shallow read but is quantitatively wrong.
decisionSpace: Treat the extract as authoritative and compute the metric directly — fastest and looks complete, but the number is wrong and would mislead planning decisions.
Flag the unit/density inconsistency, normalise to a common basis, and raise a data-quality requirement — correct and durable, but costs time and surfaces an uncomfortable finding early.

Escalate the discrepancy as a blocking data assumption and proceed on an explicitly provisional basis — keeps momentum while protecting against the error, but defers resolution and depends on the team closing it.

coverProbes.where: backlog/azure-devops-export.csv — existing 'EPIC-142 Replenishment Optimisation' owned by Solution Architecture, overlapping the new request, with stale child stories
coverProbes.reveals: A good candidate manages scope and stakeholders: checks the existing epic's status and ownership and consciously decides how their requirements relate to it rather than spawning a parallel, duplicate backlog. A naive candidate creates a fresh epic in isolation, duplicating work and stepping on the architect's ownership — exactly the solution-ownership expectation gap this role is prone to.
decisionSpace: Fold the new stories under EPIC-142 and align with the owning architect — collaborative and avoids duplication, but slower and cedes some scope control.
Raise a new epic and flag the overlap for the team to deconflict — keeps the new work clean and clearly owned, but risks two competing backlogs if deconfliction stalls.

Propose reviewing and retiring/merging the stale EPIC-142 items after confirming their status — tidies the backlog and clarifies ownership, but assumes authority to touch another team's items and needs their buy-in.
